_about: The get-started tutorial. The page walks each piece over its real screens: a step's `go` opens that screen (with `space` for an agent's own), `spot` outlines the control it's about (a CSS selector, or `text:` and the words the control starts with), and the card's Ask button starts a demo call about the piece with its `agent`. The demo call (app/tour.py) reads the same text, so both say the same. Demo content only: nothing here is anyone's real life. {donna}, {pepper} and {moneypenny} become the names of this HQ's agents.
intro: HQ is your own office, with a team in it. You call them, and they don't just talk back: they write things down, plan your days and keep things moving for you. Pick a piece below to see where things are, or try a demo call and ask whatever you want.
demo_note: Demo: everything in this tutorial is made up. Nothing you tap here changes your HQ, and nothing is saved.

pieces.title: Call your team
pieces.line: Who to call, and how a call goes

steps.title: Pick who you call
steps.text: {donna} is the quick one: your day, your list, your mail, small jobs. {pepper} takes her time: call her to plan, to think something through, or to talk about the bigger picture. {moneypenny} looks after the building of HQ. Home shows all three; tap one to open her space with everything she keeps for you.

steps.title: Tap to call
steps.text: One tap on Call and she picks up. Talk like you would on the phone. You can cut in any time, and she stops talking. The call stays on wherever you go in HQ: a bar at the top takes you back to it.

steps.title: Call me back, or call me later
steps.text: On a call, Call me back has her hang up and call you straight back, fresh, on the same call. You can also agree a time: "call me at three", or "call me when my appointment starts". Your phone then shows "{pepper} is calling", and one tap picks up. She already knows what it's about. If you miss it, {donna} tells you in her texts.

items: Call me at three about the report, okay?
Will do. I'll call you at three.

steps.title: Take it back
steps.text: Said something you didn't mean, or she heard you wrong? Take that back, on the call, takes back what you just said, before she does anything with it.

steps.title: Mute, or hold to talk
steps.text: Tap the big button at the bottom of the call to mute yourself. Hold it down to talk for as long as you want, pauses and all. Let go and she answers.

steps.title: What she's doing
steps.text: The line under her name tells you: listening, thinking or talking. While she thinks you hear a soft tick, so it's never just silence.

items: Three things. The dentist at ten, a call with Alex at two, and the report you wanted done before Friday.

steps.title: She takes it away
steps.text: Ask something that takes a long read and she says she'll look into it. A helper works on it beside the call, only reading, for a few minutes at most, and you go on talking. The answer comes back into the call, or as a text if you've hung up.

steps.title: Hang up by saying bye
steps.text: You don't have to press anything to end a call. Say bye, "that's it, see you later" or "cheers", and she says goodbye and hangs up. Her goodbye goes with what you're doing next. Hang up on the call asks once, so a stray tap never ends it.

pieces.title: Calls with more than one
pieces.line: Hand over, or bring someone in

steps.title: Hand the call over
steps.text: Calling {donna} but it's really something for {pepper}? Say "give me {pepper}". {donna} hangs up the normal way, notes and all, and {pepper} picks up right away, knowing what was said.

items: Give me {pepper}, I want to plan my week.

steps.title: Bring someone in
steps.text: Want both on the line? Say "bring in {pepper}", or tap Add someone on the call, and it's a three-way call. The one who joins says hi in her own voice, and the call shows both.

steps.title: Who answers
steps.text: With more than one on the line, the one you talk to answers. Start with her name, "{pepper}, what do you think?", or end with it. Talking about someone doesn't count, so "what do you think of {moneypenny}'s idea?" goes to whoever you asked. A plain "yes" goes to the one who spoke last.

pieces.title: What was said, and typing
pieces.line: Read back what was said, or type when you can't talk

steps.title: What was said
steps.text: On a call, the speech bubble at the top opens what was said: the whole call as text while it happens. It's different from texting her: it's this call only. Lists and bold words show up there, but she never reads the marks out loud.

steps.title: Type instead of talking
steps.text: On a train or in a library? Type under what was said and she answers out loud and in the text.

items: Remind me to buy coffee tomorrow
Done. I'll text you tomorrow morning at nine.

steps.title: A quick yes
steps.text: Looking things up never waits for you: she reads your files, HQ and this computer by herself, so she checks before she answers. She asks for your yes before she changes something, and then Yes and No show up under her question, in what was said: one tap answers, without saying a word.

steps.title: Links you can tap
steps.text: When she gives you a web link, it opens with one tap: in what was said, in past calls and in her texts. The call keeps going in the meantime. She never reads a link out loud.

steps.title: Turn her voice off
steps.text: Voice off, on the call, turns her voice off and on again, for when you'd rather read. She keeps answering in the text.

pieces.title: Your to-do list, the Eisenhower way
pieces.line: Everything to do, sorted by what really matters

steps.title: One list for everything
steps.text: Everything you have to do goes in {donna}'s To-do, in four boxes: important or not, urgent or not. Important but not urgent comes first. That's where the things are that really move your life forward, and they're the first to get pushed aside when you don't watch them.

steps.title: You just talk
steps.text: A list like this is normally a lot of admin. In HQ you just say it on a call or in a text, and it lands in the right box, in your own words. Or type it in the box under the four: one per line.

items: Learn to cook three new dishes · Plan the summer trip
Pay the tax bill by Friday

steps.title: Working with it
steps.text: Tap a box to see its list, and an item to see everything about it. Tick it off, move it, let it go, rename it, or start a call about it. Drag a row to move it up or down. Undo in the line at the top puts the last change back.

steps.title: Planned, or not yet
steps.text: On an item, Plan it in picks the block in your calendar where it gets done, from the coming two weeks. One block can hold more than one item, and on a call you just say which block. The item then shows that block's day and time, also when the block moves.

steps.title: Things that come back
steps.text: Some things come back, like a tax return every quarter or checking the rent each month. On an item, Comes back sets how often. Tick it off and it's back on its own list by itself, with its next date. Let it go and it stops.

steps.title: Groceries, done and let go
steps.text: Under the four boxes: Groceries, the Bucketlist and Wishlist, and what's done or let go. Groceries take a few at once, one per line or with commas; tick one when it's in your basket and it goes to Ticked off, ready for next time.

pieces.title: Bucketlist and wishlist
pieces.line: What you want to do, and what you'd like to have

steps.title: Two lists
steps.text: In {donna}'s Lists: the bucketlist for what you want to do once in your life, and the wishlist for what you'd like to have. Add one at the bottom of each, or just say it on a call.

steps.title: Everything about it
steps.text: Open an item for its kind, its price and how often, a goal, the hours it takes, a score, notes and links. An item can hold items of its own, each with all the same, and the totals add up.

items: A trip to the mountains · €1,200 once

pieces.title: Texts with your team
pieces.line: Reminders, heads-ups, and texting her yourself

steps.title: Her own text line
steps.text: {donna} texts you reminders at the time you asked, and a heads-up when something needs you. Text her back like in any chat app: from Texts in her space, or the box on home. Ask about something you texted earlier, even weeks back, and she looks it up. {pepper} and {moneypenny} have a line of their own too.

items: Morning. Dentist at ten, leave by half nine.
Thanks! Move my gym to tonight?

steps.title: Nudge me until it's done
steps.text: Something you keep putting off? Ask her to keep nudging you until it's done. She decides how often, more when it matters or a deadline is close, never at night. Her nudges stand at the top of her space; say done and she stops.

steps.title: A text when it starts
steps.text: On an appointment, Text me when it starts has her text you when it starts, or a few minutes before. She also does reminders outside the calendar, like "remind me at three to call the bank", and ones that come back by themselves: "remind me to drink water every two hours from 10 to 8", until you say stop.

steps.title: Let me know when
steps.text: Waiting for a parcel? Say "let me know when it's delivered" and she texts you every update from your mail, until it's there or a week has gone by. It works for the weather too: "let me know if it rains later today".

steps.title: Her own notes
steps.text: {donna}'s Notes hold your quick notes and hers: what she keeps an eye out for, the nudges that are open, and what she's waiting for.

pieces.title: Your calendar
pieces.line: Your days at a glance, planned on a call

steps.title: Your days
steps.text: Your Google Calendar inside HQ: today and the two weeks ahead, in {donna}'s Agenda. Ask on a call to plan your week, move something or block time, and she does it.

steps.title: Notes and calls on an appointment
steps.text: Tap an appointment to see it, add a note on it, or start a call about it. Your own appointments she just changes. Anything with other people in it, she asks you first.

steps.title: Done, or didn't happen
steps.text: Every appointment has Done and Didn't happen. They're kept in HQ only, nothing moves in your Google Calendar. At the end of the week you look back on a call: what got done, what didn't, and what keeps slipping.

steps.title: The five kinds, in colour
steps.text: Give an appointment a colour in Google Calendar and HQ knows what kind it is. Money makers are yellow, client delivery green, admin essentials red, CEO time blue-green, cup fillers purple, and grey is a block you haven't decided on yet. Filter, on the agenda, hides or shows a kind with a tap, and gives a kind your own name or colour. Google itself isn't changed.

items: Date night · grey, not set yet

steps.title: Travel to an appointment
steps.text: An appointment away from home gets its trip by public transport, once HQ knows where it is. In the hours before, HQ watches the live train, bus and tram info, and {donna} texts you when your train is cancelled, late or on another platform, with a 9292 link to plan again. Travel, on the appointment, turns it on or off.

items: Train from the station near home, there 13:39

pieces.title: Driving to appointments
pieces.line: By car, with the traffic, on your own maps key

steps.title: Driving to an appointment
steps.text: If you drive, a trip can go by car instead. HQ works out how long the drive takes with the traffic, and when you need to leave. From two hours before, it keeps an eye on the traffic. {donna} texts you when it's time to go, and again if the drive gets ten minutes longer or shorter. It opens in Google Maps. This one is off until you turn it on.

items: Leave by 13:15: 35 minutes by car, 8 of it traffic

steps.title: Your own maps key
steps.text: The traffic comes from a maps service, and HQ doesn't come with a key for it. You make your own once, and it stays on your computer. Two kinds work. Google Maps asks for a card, but its free monthly use covers one person's trips many times over. TomTom is free and needs no card. Pick either one, the next two steps show how.

steps.title: A Google Maps key, step by step
steps.text: 1. Go to console.cloud.google.com and sign in with your Google account. 2. At the top, make a new project, called HQ for example. 3. Open Billing and add a card (Google asks for it; the free use covers HQ). Under Budgets and alerts, set a small budget, like 5 euros, so you hear about it if anything ever costs money. 4. Open APIs and Services, Library, search for Routes API, and press Enable. 5. Open APIs and Services, Credentials, Create credentials, API key. 6. Press Edit on the new key: under API restrictions pick Restrict key, tick only the Routes API, and Save. 7. Copy the key. It starts with AIza.

steps.title: Or TomTom, free without a card
steps.text: 1. Go to developer.tomtom.com and press Register. 2. Fill in your name and email, and confirm the email they send you. 3. Sign in. Your dashboard already has a key on the Keys page. 4. Copy it. The free plan gives 2,500 looks a day. HQ uses about a dozen per trip and never more than 150 a day.

steps.title: Paste it in
steps.text: Open Settings, What HQ helps you with, and turn on Driving to appointments. A box shows up under it: paste your key and press Save. It's kept on this computer only, never in your files and never uploaded. Running two HQs? Paste it on both. Forget takes it off again. Never say or type your key on a call or in a text.

steps.title: On each appointment
steps.text: Open an appointment away from home and tap Travel. With only driving on, every trip goes by car. With public transport on too, a trip starts by public transport and can switch to the car. Or just say it on a call: go by car to the dentist.

pieces.title: Quick notes
pieces.line: Jot something down for later

steps.title: A quick note
steps.text: A thought you don't want to lose? Write it in Notes. The next call can read your notes, so you can say: let's go through my notes. Cleared one by mistake? Undo right after, or Put back from the cleared ones: nothing you clear is lost.

items: Ask about the new running shoes
Idea: a picnic in the park

pieces.title: Past calls
pieces.line: Every call kept, to read back or carry on

steps.title: Every call kept
steps.text: Every call is saved as text, in Past calls in each agent's space. Open one and read it back, or carry it on and she picks up where you left off, knowing what was said. If a call dropped, the end of it says so, so a drop is never written down as you hanging up.

pieces.title: The mail check
pieces.line: HQ reads your new mail every hour

steps.title: Every hour, quietly
steps.text: Every hour HQ reads your new mail and keeps only what might need you, in {donna}'s Mail. The very important things, like a bill with a date or someone waiting for your answer, you hear at the start of every call until you say it's sorted. HQ never sends mail. Drafts at the most, and you send them yourself.

items: Your parcel is on its way

steps.title: Check more often for a while
steps.text: Waiting for something important? Say "check my mail more often until tonight", or for a few hours, or until Friday. HQ then looks every fifteen minutes, and goes back to once an hour by itself when the time's up.

steps.title: Tidy your mail
steps.text: Ask {donna} to tidy up: mark mail read, archive it, star it, or put a label on it. She makes and renames labels too. The trash only when you ask for exactly that.

steps.title: Sorted from now on
steps.text: Want a kind of mail sorted from now on, like all your receipts in one label? {donna} gives you two ways. She walks you through making a real Gmail filter, step by step. Or you agree a sorting rule with her, and the hourly mail check puts new mail in its label for you. You can see your rules, and stop one any time.

pieces.title: Weather and rain
pieces.line: The weather at a glance, a text before the rain

steps.title: The weather
steps.text: The weather where you are, at the top of home. Tap it for more: the next hours, today and tomorrow, the wind and its gusts, and the rain radar for the next two hours. An official weather warning shows in there in full.

steps.title: Rain while you're out
steps.text: When you wake up, {donna} tells you if it'll rain while you're out today. Turn on Rain alerts and she also texts before a shower would catch you outside, and keeps following it as it moves. While you sleep, she says nothing.

steps.title: Let me know between 2 and 6
steps.text: Going out at a time that's not in your calendar? Tell her "let me know between 2 and 6", once or every day, and she watches the rain for those hours.

pieces.title: Settings
pieces.line: The design, voices, sound, light or dark, and what HQ helps you with

steps.title: Three designs
steps.text: Settings, Design, picks how HQ looks: Spotlight, one of the three at a time; Thread, HQ as three conversations; or Desk, the three side by side. Everything else stays the same.

steps.title: Light or dark
steps.text: Look picks Light or Dark, or System to follow your phone or computer. HQ keeps it that way on this device.

steps.title: Voices and sound
steps.text: Change a voice gives each agent her own. Microphone and sound picks your microphone, where her voice comes out, and the soft thinking sound. On a Mac, Other sound says whether your music turns down during a call.

steps.title: What HQ helps you with
steps.text: Every part of HQ is a switch: the calendar, the to-do list, texts, the weather, travel by public transport, the mail check, notes, and Life coaching. Turn off what you don't use. Driving to appointments starts off, because it needs your own maps key.

steps.title: Free
steps.text: Free mode is plain Claude with only the web: none of your files, and nothing is saved. Handy when you want to show HQ to someone without showing your life.

pieces.title: Life coaching
pieces.line: Your long-term vision, one calm session at a time

steps.title: Your vision, layer by layer
steps.text: With Life coaching on, {pepper}'s map goes from the life you want in three to five years, down to this year, a six-week game, your ideal week and this week. Each layer has its checklist: what's answered, what's left for later, and what's still open. You give your vision its own name.

steps.title: One session per layer
steps.text: Open a layer and start it: {pepper} calls about only that one, one question at a time, and writes your answers down in your own words. Short sessions, so nothing drifts off.

steps.title: Check-ins
steps.text: HQ keeps the moments to look back: every week, at the end of a game, and a bigger check-in every eight weeks, in step with the games. When one is due, {pepper}'s card says so. Her coaching line is a chat with her just for life coaching.

pieces.title: Your six-week game
pieces.line: One simple game you can win, six weeks at a time

steps.title: A game you can win
steps.text: In Life coaching you design a six-week game with {pepper}: one simple thing, like moving every day. Once it's set up, her space shows where you are, the win line, and how far along you are.

steps.title: Tick it off
steps.text: Tick today off in the game, or just say it on a call or text {donna}. The weeks run Monday to Sunday with each day's date; today is outlined, and days outside the game are greyed. Add how it felt, or a note, when you want.

steps.title: Look back and keep it
steps.text: Every week you look back on it, and at the end there's a short debrief: was it fun, was it useful, what did you learn. Past games are kept, so you can open them again.

pieces.title: Building HQ with {moneypenny}
pieces.line: Hand-overs, how HQ is doing, and updates

steps.title: Hand-overs
steps.text: {moneypenny} prepares the work for building HQ: a hand-over, ready for you and Claude Code to build together. The newest is under her card; all of them are in Hand-overs.

steps.title: Status
steps.text: Status shows what's being worked on, your Claude usage for the 5-hour and the week, the planning board to look at, work sessions, health and updates.

steps.title: Health
steps.text: Health lists every routine with its light, what HQ can't read in red, the graphs of the last hours, the laptop's temperature and battery, and what went down, why and when it came back. Turn everything on starts what's off.

steps.title: The lid
steps.text: On a laptop, Health has a switch on the lid's line: one tap and it keeps working with the lid closed. Tap again and it goes to sleep like normal.

pieces.title: HQ on your phone
pieces.line: Call your computer from anywhere

steps.title: Nothing to install on the phone
steps.text: HQ runs on your computer, or on a server. Your phone just calls it. It reaches your computer privately through Tailscale, a free app, with nothing open to the internet.

steps.title: Connect it, step by step
steps.text: 1. Install Tailscale on your computer and on your phone, and sign in on both with the same account. 2. On the phone, open the address your Claude gave you after the install in Safari. It ends in .ts.net:8443. 3. Allow the microphone. That's it, you can call.

steps.title: Put it on your home screen
steps.text: In Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen. HQ's icon lands next to your other apps and opens like an app. Opened from there, her texts can show up on your lock screen once you allow notifications.

steps.title: Going back
steps.text: On the phone, swipe from the left edge to go back one screen, and pull a sheet down to close it.

pieces.title: HQ on a server
pieces.line: Always on, also when your laptop is closed

steps.title: Why a server
steps.text: A laptop goes to sleep. A small server never does, so your mail keeps getting checked while your laptop is closed. HQ runs on a Linux server just like on a Mac. Everything works there, except what's about a laptop, like the battery and the lid.

steps.title: Getting it there
steps.text: The steps are the same as on a Mac: install Claude Code on the server, get HQ, and ask Claude to install everything. It tells you plainly what's missing and the line to fix it. You then call it from your phone or laptop through Tailscale, the same way.

pieces.title: Two HQs: main and backup
pieces.line: Your laptop and a server, working as one

steps.title: One main, one backup
steps.text: Have HQ on your laptop and on a server? They can work as one. The main one does the work: the mail check, the reminders, the planned things. The backup takes your calls too and passes anything you agree on to the main one. Your files are the same on both within seconds.

steps.title: Which one is main
steps.text: Health and Status say which HQ this is, and whether it's the main one or the backup, and which one is main. On the backup, Health has the hand-over switch: whether it passes what it holds to the main every minute.

steps.title: When one goes away
steps.text: If the main one goes offline, the backup takes over by itself after five minutes, and hands back when the main one returns. Want to switch yourself? Just say it on a call: make the server main. It switches right away, or as soon as the running job is done.

pieces.title: Updates
pieces.line: What's new, and getting it

steps.title: What's new
steps.text: Updates, under {moneypenny}'s Status, shows the version you're on and what's new in every version. Check now looks for a newer one.

steps.title: The Update button
steps.text: HQ looks a few times a day for a new version. When there is one, a bar on home says what's new with an Update button, and Not now hides it until the next version. One tap and it updates and restarts what it needs to, without restarting your computer. A call in progress ends, so tap it when you're off a call. Your own files and what you built yourself are never touched.

steps.title: Going back a version
steps.text: If a new version turns out bad, one command takes HQ back one version, on both your computers, and undoes what that version changed in your data. Ask your agent, or run python3 routine/update.py back. It goes forward again with python3 routine/update.py forward.

pieces.title: Make it yours
pieces.line: HQ is built to grow

steps.title: Your own headquarters
steps.text: This is why HQ was built: so everyone can have their own headquarters, with their own team behind them. What's in it now is what its maker thought most people would want. His own HQ has a lot more, and people testing it have already built their own.

steps.title: Updates never break your own
steps.text: What you add yourself is an extension. It lives in your own files, and an update never touches it. After every update HQ checks whether something you added might not fit the new version. If so, a bar on home says which one, with two buttons: Talk it through with {donna}, or It's fine. What you add can bring its own checks: HQ runs them every night with its own, on a throwaway copy.

facts: HQ runs on your own computer, on your own Claude plan, through Claude Code. Your voice is turned into text on your computer, and her voice is made there too. Only the thinking goes to Anthropic, the same as any Claude chat.
Your phone reaches your computer privately, through Tailscale, with nothing open to the internet. Add HQ to your phone's home screen and it works like an app. There's a Mac app too.
Your own files live in your workspace, a folder of plain text files on your computer. They're never uploaded with HQ, and updates never touch them.

HQ is still being built. One person built it and uses it every day, and now it's shared with friends. Under Moneypenny, Status, Updates shows the version you're on and what's new; a bar on home shows when a new version is out.
The routine is a small helper that runs every minute without Claude, so waiting costs nothing. A watchdog brings things back when they stop.
Things that need your yes, like an appointment with other people in it or anything with your mail, are checked with you first. Mail is never sent.
After a real call, the text of it is saved and the call's notes go in your log, in your own words. Free calls and demo calls are never saved.

Travel on appointments uses open data, free and without a key: the live train, bus, tram and metro info the Dutch transport companies publish (through OVapi), the government's address service, and 9292 links. Driving is its own feature, on your own Google Maps or TomTom key, kept on your computer; HQ doesn't come with a key and counts its looks, at most 150 a day.

When an agent calls you at a time you agreed, it comes as a notification on your phone, not a real phone call: an app like this can't ring like a phone, and HQ uses no paid phone service. One tap on it opens HQ and the call starts.
Running HQ on a server and on a laptop at once is set up by your Claude once both are installed; the steps are in INSTALL.md. Windows has no ready version yet.

HQ comes in three designs: Spotlight (one of the three at a time, swipe between them), Thread (HQ as three conversations) and Desk (the three side by side, today underneath). Settings, Design switches between them, and everything else stays the same.
